items.title: Commodities are pricing a full recession in everything physical
items.idea: Paulo says positioning across copper, wheat, PGMs, oil and uranium is discounting 'a full-blown recession in everything': grid capex, calories, ICE/hybrid demand, fuel, nuclear fuel. In copper and uranium he sees positioning and sentiment unmatched since Covid, while years of underinvestment remain. His conclusion: we are likely already in a recession few had on their bingo card.
items.angle: Pairs with Boockvar's uranium spot/equity gap and CAT -46%: the market is liquidating physical-economy exposure regardless of inventory. Washed-out spec length is the setup for a squeeze once the AI unwind finishes.
items.tweetA: Copper, wheat, platinum, oil and uranium all positioned for recession at once. Food doesn't usually go into the recession bin with copper. When everything physical gets degrossed together, it's a liquidity event, not a demand forecast.
items.tweetB: Either the physical economy is collapsing across grids, calories and fuel at the same time, or AI-unwind de-risking is dragging commodity books down with it. Inventories will tell you which one. I'm betting on the second.

charts.desc: Positioning charts on copper and wheat, plus a 2022 Bloomberg 'Rise of the Bottlenecks' chart. Positioning vs. inventory is the one to save.

items.title: Bottleneck economy: next upturn hits the inflation wall sooner than 1980-2020
items.idea: Paulo revives a 2022 Bloomberg 'Rise of the Bottlenecks' chart: supply constraints that started in Covid are still there. In a populist, deglobalizing nominal economy, once growth turns up, price discovery is immediate and inflation arrives much faster than in the 1980-2020 regime. Copper is the most extreme case: positioning vs. inventory and visible supply growth is 'absurd'.
items.angle: The recession trade and the next inflation trade are the same trade, a few quarters apart. Underowned copper and uranium producers are long-dated calls on the rebound.
items.tweetA: Recession today, bottleneck inflation tomorrow. Nobody's adding copper capacity while specs dump the contract. The upturn after this will reprice supply in weeks, not years.
items.tweetB: The 1980-2020 playbook assumed supply was elastic. It isn't anymore. If the next cycle's inflation shows up in quarter one of the recovery, today's commodity washout is the entry.

charts.desc: 2022 Bloomberg chart: supply bottlenecks by category.

items.title: The yen is becoming the anti-AI currency
items.idea: USD/JPY can't hold 160 even with US 2y above 4.8%, and Japan Q3 GDP contracted 0.1% annualized. Innes says the yen is gaining from two things: a BoJ still about 85% priced for a December hike, and a global unwind of AI-funded risk. His AUD/JPY short from 109.40 is up about 200 pips.
items.angle: With NVDA reporting after the close, JPY crosses are the cleanest macro hedge on the AI tape. A weak print plus a December BoJ hike would squeeze carry hard.
items.tweetA: Japan just printed a negative GDP quarter and the yen still won't break 160. When bad domestic data can't sink a currency, something bigger is buying it. That's the AI carry unwind. $FXY
items.tweetB: If NVDA disappoints tonight, I'm watching AUD/JPY, not the Nasdaq futures. The funding currency of the AI boom is quietly becoming its hedge.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: EUR/USD broke 1.10 and nobody cared: dollar's easy money is gone
items.idea: EUR/USD slipped under 1.1000 after earlier breaks of 1.12 and 1.11, but the euro recovered as the front-end differential narrowed about 5bp. DXY is above 103.50, the US 2y is above 4.8%, and Hammack left the door open to outsized hikes. Even so, the AI selloff has brought dovish repricing without hurting the dollar, because defensive demand is offsetting it.
items.angle: The dollar is now supported by flight-to-safety, not carry. If the selloff gets deep enough to pull the front end down hard, both supports fail together.
items.tweetA: A Fed open to outsized hikes and EUR/USD can't hold under 1.10. When a hawkish central bank can't extend a break, the positioning is full.
items.tweetB: The dollar's two pillars are hawkish carry and safe-haven demand from the AI rout. A bad enough NVDA print kills the first and caps the second. Respect the trend, but stop adding.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: China Oct: retail sales +0.4%, FAI -8.1% YTD, exports still carrying the yuan
items.idea: China's October retail sales slowed to 0.4% y/y, IP eased to 4.8% from 5.5%, and fixed-asset investment is down 8.1% over ten months. Exports and corporate FX conversion are still holding the yuan up. Innes warns against treating weak data as an automatic short-CNY signal.
items.angle: A domestic economy this weak plus a strong currency is the deflation-export setup Europe hates. Expect more trade friction, not less, into the Trump-Xi Shenzhen meeting.
items.tweetA: China fixed-asset investment down 8.1% YTD. Retail sales at +0.4%. The only engine left is selling to the rest of us, right before Trump sits down with Xi.
items.tweetB: Weak domestic demand plus a firm yuan means China exports deflation and keeps the FX gains. Europe takes the hit first. Watch EU anti-dumping cases, not the CNY fix.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Thailand's two-speed economy: exports +18.3%, consumption +2.5%
items.idea: Thai Q3 GDP rose to 2.9% y/y, with exports up 18.3% and investment up 11.8% on the AI electronics cycle. Household consumption grew only 2.5%, sequential GDP was 0.3%, and the policy rate is 1%. Innes flags the dependence on AI capex at the moment its durability is in doubt.
items.angle: Thailand is one of the five countries now under BIS license requirements (per ChinaTalk), so its AI export engine is exposed to both the capex slowdown and export controls. That's a double hit.
items.tweetA: Thai exports +18.3% on the AI cycle. Thailand also just landed on the BIS chip-license list. The country's growth engine is now exposed to two different AI shocks.
items.tweetB: When consumption grows 2.5% and exports grow 18%, the economy is a derivative of someone else's capex. Southeast Asia's AI boom was partly China's rerouted demand. That pipe is being shut.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Global tightening: ECB pricing ~70bp of hikes, BoJ 85% for December
items.idea: Markets price about 70bp of ECB tightening over the next year (next move after December not until March) and roughly 85% odds of a December BoJ hike. The Fed is in a 'prolonged tightening cycle' narrative. French fiscal risk and Le Pen's pension plan are extra euro risks, and lower oil could bring dovish ECB repricing.
items.angle: A synchronized global hiking cycle during an AI equity unwind is the 2018 Q4 template. Front-end receivers outside the US are the convexity play if the selloff deepens.
items.tweetA: Fed, ECB and BoJ all priced to hike at the same time AI equities are unwinding. Last time the world tightened into a growth scare was Q4 2018, and that ended with a pivot in January.
items.tweetB: 70bp of ECB hikes priced, oil falling, Le Pen talking pensions. One of those has to give, and it won't be the pricing that wins.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Huang-over spreads: Taiwan, Korea -1%, YTL Power -10%
items.idea: Taiwan and Korea tech-heavy indices fell more than 1% Tuesday, and Nvidia partner YTL Power (Malaysia) plunged nearly 10%. Innes says the rout started on Wall Street and is now forcing a rethink of positions built on endlessly expanding AI capex. NVDA's first print without Huang and Anthropic's IPO are this week's tests.
items.angle: YTL Power is the most direct listed exposure to the Johor neocloud buildout that the new BIS rental cap targets. That's the clearest single-name read-through from the BIS rule.
items.tweetA: YTL Power -10% in a day. It's the Malaysian Nvidia partner building Johor data centers, the exact capacity the new BIS rule stops renting to China. The market priced the export rule before most people read it.
items.tweetB: Asia is paying Wall Street's AI bar tab, and the pain is in the neocloud landlords, not the chipmakers. If Johor capacity has to find US tenants, check what that does to rental rates.

items.title: Five setups worth trading: let the market show its hand, then enter where risk is smallest
items.idea: PaperAlfa narrows technical analysis to five setups: two continuation patterns and three 'second-chance' entries. All share one principle: wait for the market to move, pause, and confirm, then enter where the stop is tight and the exit is obvious. They work across rates, FX, equities and commodities because they describe behaviour, not instruments. Volume confirmation is central.
items.angle: In a regime of violent AI-unwind reversals, second-chance entries beat chasing the first break. EUR/USD's shrug at 1.10 is a live example of a failed first break.
items.tweetA: Most chart patterns are noise. The ones that work have one thing in common: you're not predicting, you're waiting for the market to confirm what it already did, then paying the smallest possible stop to join.
items.tweetB: In a tape where every gap gets faded (EUR/USD at 1.10 yesterday), the first break is for tourists. The second-chance entry is where risk/reward actually lives.

charts.desc: Five annotated drawn examples of the setups (entries, stops, targets).

items.title: Compounding works in reverse: a VC on losing the habit loop
items.idea: Marvin Liao says a stretch of travel across 7+ countries in Q2-Q3 2026 broke his training routine from June, and the drop compounded into clarity, health and confidence. His fix: 'eat the frog' by training first thing in the morning, because anything pushed to the afternoon gets crowded out. The core idea is that habits compound negatively exactly as fast as positively.
items.angle: A soft piece, but the theme applies to portfolio process: skipped reviews and drifting risk rules compound the same way.
items.tweetA: Compounding is symmetric. Skip the gym for three weeks and you don't lose three weeks, you lose the slope. Same with risk process: the drawdown starts the week you stop doing the boring checks.
items.tweetB: A VC's 2026 travel calendar broke his routine by June. The founder/investor class is spending more time in airports than ever. That's a quiet tax on judgement.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Goldman 2027 Gold)
items.title: Goldman 2027 gold: central banks set the trend, the Fed sets the next $100
items.idea: Goldman's Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven see a familiar pattern: central-bank and China buying underpins the long-term bull market, while Fed rate expectations drive day-to-day swings. The bullish year-end target comes with a warning: a hawkish Fed could delay recovery. Gold is now one of the most-traded retail CFD instruments, which is part of why it has become so violent. Spot is around $3,870.
items.angle: This splits gold into two markets: price-insensitive official buyers below, leveraged retail on top. Dips caused by Fed hawkishness flush the CFD crowd into central-bank bids.
items.tweetA: Gold now has two owners: central banks who don't care about price and CFD traders who only care about price. Goldman's outlook says the first sets direction and the second sets volatility. Trade accordingly.
items.tweetB: Gold at $3,870 with the Fed talking about outsized hikes. If real rates can't break the official bid, the old rates model for gold is dead and Goldman just quietly admitted it. $GLD

items.tweetA: Silver squeezed, everyone learned 'silver squeezes'. Goldman's warning is that the conditions behind that squeeze don't repeat on demand.
items.tweetB: Thornton is buying silver, PauloMacro calls PGM positioning recessionary, Goldman warns squeeze lessons don't carry over. Precious metals haven't been this split in years.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: BIS 132-page rule closes three compute loopholes at once
items.idea: Monday's rule (Commerce credited Treasury and the NSC as authors) does three things: license requirements for AI chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil; a cap on compute rented to Chinese firms; and re-closing the TSMC foundry backdoor. McGuire says it will steer 'hundreds of billions of dollars of capital flows'. Chinese clients get about 90 days, after which only recommendation-engine workloads are allowed.
items.angle: This changes Asian neocloud economics, not NVDA's near-term unit demand. Those GPUs need new tenants, and Western labs will be bidding for them.
items.tweetA: Commerce publishing a rule and crediting Treasury and the NSC as authors is the tell. Washington doesn't trust Commerce to enforce its own controls. That matters more than the 132 pages.
items.tweetB: 90 days. After that, Johor's GPU farms can't serve Chinese clients beyond recommendation engines. Somebody has to fill those racks. I'd be calling the neoclouds today if I ran a frontier lab.

charts.desc: ChinaTalk's April breakdown of China compute by source: domestic, smuggled, legal foreign, remote access.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: About 2/5 of China's AI compute is rented remotely, and the cap is ~200 Blackwells
items.idea: Per ChinaTalk's estimate, about two-fifths of China's total AI compute comes from remote access. The rule caps license-free rentals to Chinese firms at about 200 top Blackwells or 800 H100s. The rule is retroactive: providing over half your compute to Chinese companies was 'always' a violation, which could expose Megaspeed.
items.angle: A 200-GPU cap against frontier training runs of 100k+ GPUs is roughly 0.2%, so it's effectively a ban. The freed supply is a near-term tailwind for US labs' compute access.
items.tweetA: The cap is about 200 Blackwells. A frontier training run uses 100,000+. That's 0.2% of one run. This isn't a limit, it's a ban that's labelled as a limit.
items.tweetB: If 40% of China's AI compute is rented and that gets cut, it's the biggest supply shock to Chinese AI since the 2022 controls, and it lands right as DeepSeek-class labs need to scale inference.

charts.desc: China compute mix chart (domestic / smuggled / legal foreign / remote access). This one is the story.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: The Northern Virginia loophole: rental cap stops at the US border
items.idea: The rental cap doesn't apply inside the United States. McGuire warns Chinese firms will move rented compute from Johor to Northern Virginia, making it 'the center of China AI until we fix this'. Commerce has the authority to close it now. Until then, Chinese firms will compete for the most oversubscribed data center capacity in the world.
items.angle: A short-term spike in demand for US colo capacity from Chinese tenants is plausible, with a follow-up rule as the overhang. Watch for disclosures from DC REITs and neoclouds.
items.tweetA: New export rule: Chinese companies can't rent GPUs in Malaysia. They can rent them in Ashburn. Northern Virginia is about to become China's biggest AI cluster.
items.tweetB: If the loophole stays open, Chinese labs bid against OpenAI and Anthropic for US colo. That raises AI compute costs for everyone. If it closes, US neocloud demand drops. Both outcomes are priced nowhere.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: TSMC license for any Chinese chip at 14nm or below: Xiaomi needs permission, Qualcomm wins
items.idea: The rule requires any Chinese company making a chip at 14nm or more advanced at TSMC to get a license, AI or not. Xiaomi would now need a license for a 3nm smartphone chip. McGuire says this is good for Qualcomm and other US firms selling phone chips to China. The aim is to block circumvention, since China illicitly made 'millions of chips' at TSMC.
items.angle: This is an underappreciated positive for $QCOM and $MediaTek-style merchant SoC suppliers, and a negative for Chinese in-house silicon programs (Xiaomi XRING) and TSMC's China revenue.
items.tweetA: Buried in the BIS rule: every Chinese chip at 14nm or below made at TSMC now needs a US license, AI or not. Xiaomi's 3nm phone chip just became a Commerce Department decision. $QCOM
items.tweetB: Everyone reads this rule as an AI rule. It's also a smartphone rule. Chinese OEMs designing their own SoCs at TSMC now face a license queue. Merchant chip vendors get the share back.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: Southeast Asia: 3rd, 4th, 5th and 8th largest AI chip importers relative to GDP
items.idea: Relative to GDP, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia were the 3rd, 4th, 5th and 8th largest AI chip importers in the world. McGuire says they 'basically displaced China'. Brazil was added because of large data centers for ByteDance. He expects smuggling to move to Bhutan, Nepal or elsewhere, and calls for US visibility or a veto on any purchase of hundreds of millions of dollars in AI chips anywhere.
items.angle: Rerouted demand to SEA was a big part of the Asian AI export boom (see Thailand exports +18.3%). Licensing ends the 'neutral third country' trade.
items.tweetA: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia were among the top-8 AI chip importers per unit of GDP. Nobody believed those were domestic workloads. Now they need licenses.
items.tweetB: Brazil is on the BIS list because of ByteDance data centers. The export-control map is now drawn by where Chinese hyperscalers rent racks, not by geography.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: Jensen's soup vendor: why Nvidia wanted China
items.idea: Per a WSJ account McGuire cites, Huang told neocloud CEOs about a Japanese soup vendor who refused to sell a second bowl to keep prices high and customers diverse. McGuire's read: Nvidia fears concentration in a few hyperscalers who could switch to AMD or in-house chips. At Nvidia's scale, the only other large customer base is China (or the Gulf). He adds that export controls 'have not negatively impacted a single Nvidia sale'.
items.angle: Customer concentration is NVDA's real long-term risk, and the China channel was the hedge. Closing it raises hyperscaler bargaining power and custom-ASIC share ($AVGO, $MRVL).
items.tweetA: Nvidia's China push was never about China. It was about not depending on five hyperscalers who are all building their own chips. Close China and you hand bargaining power to the custom-ASIC teams. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: 'Export controls haven't cost Nvidia a single sale.' True while demand exceeded supply. SemiAnalysis just cut accelerator spend about 30%. The day supply exceeds demand, China access becomes the swing factor.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: 3M Huawei chips from TSMC, $45B, zero consequences: export controls need a BNP moment
items.idea: McGuire estimates Huawei made 3 million AI chips at TSMC, which at $15k each is about $45B of product, with no consequences so far. Applied Materials' $500M fine is 'a drop in the bucket'. Banks only changed after BNP Paribas's $9B fine. Commerce reportedly knew about the smuggling for months. Expect discovery, shareholder suits and congressional probes.
items.angle: Enforcement risk is a new tail for the whole semi supply chain (fabs, server ODMs, toolmakers). Fines on the BNP scale would hit balance sheets, not just headlines.
items.tweetA: Huawei got about $45B of AI chips out of TSMC. The biggest export-control fine to date is $500M. Until a chip company pays a BNP-sized $9B, the rules are a suggestion. $TSM $AMAT
items.tweetB: Banks ignored sanctions until one paid $9B. The chip supply chain is in its pre-BNP era. Discovery from the Nvidia lawsuits could be what changes that. Server ODMs should be nervous.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: Hundreds of thousands of H200s stuck in Hong Kong port, and the Shenzhen summit
items.idea: Beijing is leaving 'hundreds of thousands of H200s' in Hong Kong port, which the administration cites as evidence China doesn't need the access, while pushing for Blackwell approvals. A senior official said 'we don't negotiate on export controls'. Gewirtz's base case: Beijing bets on Trump softening the regime at Shenzhen, as it did after the AI diffusion rule. He also asks whether Xi even knows how dependent Chinese labs are on foreign compute.
items.angle: The binary is whether Trump trades the rule away in Shenzhen. A rollback would reflate the Asian neocloud and SEA export complex. Holding firm extends the hit to Chinese model labs.
items.tweetA: China is refusing H200s sitting in its own port while lobbying for Blackwells. That's not a country short of compute. It's a country negotiating for the better chip.
items.tweetB: Last time Washington tightened AI chip rules, Beijing just waited for Trump to loosen them. The rule dropped days before Shenzhen. I'd price at least 40% odds of a quiet carve-out.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ McGuire & Gewirtz
items.title: Frontier labs are calling around for the compute China just lost
items.idea: McGuire says multiple AI labs contacted him the morning the rule landed, asking who was most affected so they could buy the compute. Andy Jassy and Elon Musk both say they can't get enough chips. Gewirtz notes much of China's remote-access use was company-driven while the state looked away, and DeepSeek's founder admitted using 'unlicensed cards'.
items.angle: Near-term this is reallocation, not demand destruction: SEA neocloud capacity reprices to Western tenants. It slightly undercuts SemiAnalysis's 30% capex cut thesis.
items.tweetA: Within hours of the BIS rule, US AI labs were asking which Asian neoclouds lost Chinese tenants so they could rent the GPUs. The AI 'glut' lasted one morning.
items.tweetB: SemiAnalysis cuts accelerator spend 30%. The same week, labs are cold-calling Malaysian data centers for spare capacity. One is a 2027 forecast, the other is today's order book.

items.title: Global liquidity flat at $196.2tn, but the Shadow Monetary Base is falling
items.idea: Howell's weekly: global liquidity has stabilized around $196.2tn, but underlying momentum is weakening as the Shadow Monetary Base falls. Supportive funding conditions and a stable collateral multiplier are offsetting a stronger dollar, weaker collateral values and ongoing ECB/BoJ QT. Risk appetite recovered last week, favouring DM, while the rotation out of EM, especially China, continued.
items.angle: The headline number hides a deteriorating core. Funding plumbing is propping up the total, which leaves little buffer if repo or collateral values crack during the AI unwind.
items.tweetA: $196tn of global liquidity, flat. The base underneath is shrinking, and repo plumbing is holding up the headline. That's how 2019 looked right before the repo spike.
items.tweetB: Strong dollar, falling collateral values, ECB and BoJ still in QT, and the market thinks liquidity is fine because the total isn't falling. Watch the components, not the sum.

items.source: The Market House / Maggie Lake (Tom Thornton)
items.title: QQQ took a record $13.4B in one week while institutions de-risked
items.idea: Tom Thornton: institutions have cut risk substantially, retail has not. QQQ took in about $13.43B during Nov 9-13, the largest weekly inflow ever, as retail 'bought the living daylights out of tech all the way down'. He calls this how tops develop: buy-the-dip works, then stops working. If NVDA cuts guidance even slightly, he expects a retail washout.
items.angle: Record retail inflows into a falling Nasdaq are the opposite of capitulation. Combine with Situational Awareness's 92% AUM collapse: smart money is out, retail is in.
items.tweetA: Record week for QQQ inflows, $13.4B, in the middle of an AI drawdown. Bottoms don't form on record inflows. They form on the 'hand on face' NYSE trader photo.
items.tweetB: Leopold's fund went from $20B to $1.6B. QQQ took in a record $13B in one week. The professionals who were most AI-bullish are gone, and retail took their seats. $QQQ $NVDA

items.source: The Market House / Maggie Lake (Tom Thornton)
items.title: Thornton: NVDA's problems are legal, not cyclical
items.idea: Thornton says Nvidia faces DOJ and Congress, and if documents show it knew chips went to China, 'that is jail time'. Circular financing deals Huang made are under stress with him gone. For tonight's earnings, any guidance cut 'below 0%' would wash retail out. He sees 2027 as a 'rougher year', sees DeMark exhaustion signals in NDX/Mag7 as not yet complete, and sees sell signals in staples and utilities.
items.angle: The circular-financing book (neocloud equity stakes, backstops) is the hidden balance-sheet risk post-Huang. Watch the earnings commentary on commitments, not revenue.
items.tweetA: Tonight's NVDA number matters less than one line: what happens to the circular financing deals Jensen signed now that Jensen isn't there to honour them? $NVDA
items.tweetB: Thornton is selling staples and utilities and waiting on NVDA. If the defensive trade is also exhausted, there's nowhere to hide except cash and yen.

items.title: SemiAnalysis cut its AI accelerator spend estimate by almost 30%
items.idea: Boockvar flags that SemiAnalysis cut its AI accelerator spend estimate by almost 30%, citing a slower data center build after the midterms, a higher cost of capital, and lower frontier-lab token revenue expectations. He repeats his call: 2026 is peak rate-of-change in data center capex and 2027 is peak dollars. NVDA is ultimately a picks-and-shovels stock tied to industry capex, beyond the CEO change and China.
items.angle: The most important AI datapoint of the week landed the day before NVDA earnings. If the most bullish independent shop cuts 30%, sell-side 2027 numbers are stale.
items.tweetA: SemiAnalysis, which was the most bullish AI capex shop, just cut accelerator spend 30%. When the bulls' own model breaks, the sell side is still behind. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: Three inputs to the cut: midterms, cost of capital, lab token revenue. Only the third is about AI. The other two are politics and rates. The AI capex cycle turned into a macro trade.

items.title: Uranium spot $90, term price a record ~$100, equities crushed
items.idea: Uranium spot is steady around $90/lb and long-term contract prices are near a record $100/lb. Uranium equities have still been crushed because investors lump nuclear in with the data center trade. Boockvar is long and argues nuclear's case (24/7 clean baseload and energy independence after the Middle East conflict) goes far beyond AI.
items.angle: The clearest price-vs-equity divergence on the board. Paulo also sees Covid-level washed-out uranium positioning. Two independent sources point to the same mispricing.
items.tweetA: Uranium term price: record high. Uranium stocks: crushed. The commodity didn't care about the AI unwind. The equity holders did. $CCJ $URA
items.tweetB: Boockvar sees the spot/equity gap and PauloMacro sees Covid-level washed-out uranium positioning, on the same morning. When the producers' price is at a record and the stocks trade like it's 2020, that's a gap.

items.title: Asian picks-and-shovels sold off overnight on new China rules
items.idea: Boockvar notes that the data center supply chain in Asia sold off overnight on the tighter rules around selling to China directly or indirectly. US data center construction may slow, and Asia's is about to as well, since China is a large customer.
items.angle: Read with Innes (YTL Power -10%) and ChinaTalk (SEA licensing): the BIS rule is a capex shock for Asian suppliers before it touches NVDA's reported numbers.
items.tweetA: The BIS rule hits Asian data-center suppliers before it hits Nvidia's income statement. The overnight selloff in Taiwan, Korea and Malaysia is the first-order effect.
items.tweetB: US capex slowing after the midterms plus Asian capex losing its China customer. That's two legs of the data-center demand stool cut in the same week.

items.title: What doctors and influencers are telling us to do (section teaser)
items.idea: The email's headline promises a section on doctors' and influencers' health advice, but the free preview ends before it. Only the title is visible.
items.angle: Placeholder only. Open the full post if consumer health / GLP-1 / wellness spending themes are relevant.
items.tweetA: When a macro strategist adds a section on what doctors and influencers tell people to do, it's usually about spending. Health advice is now a consumer-spending variable.
items.tweetB: Health influencers move more consumer dollars than most ad campaigns. Worth tracking when a macro writer starts noticing.

items.source: David Rosenberg / Early Morning with Dave
items.title: CAT -46% from the June highs: the AI build-out's bellwether cracks
items.idea: Caterpillar fell another 5% and is down 46% from its late-June highs. Rosenberg says the old-economy industrial became an AI proxy because it supplies the gas turbines and large engines for on-site primary and backup data center power. Its collapse signals investors pricing a peak in the data center construction curve.
items.angle: CAT leads NVDA because power is ordered before chips arrive. A 46% drawdown in the power supplier is a 2-3 quarter lead on GPU orders.
items.tweetA: CAT is down 46% from June. Data centers order turbines and gensets before they order GPUs. If the power gear is getting cancelled, the chip orders follow two or three quarters later. $CAT $NVDA
items.tweetB: A 100-year-old equipment company became an AI stock in 2025 and lost half its value in five months. That's what happens when industrials trade on someone else's capex story. Check $GEV and $VRT next.

items.title: CFTC approves Backpack as first onchain DCM + DCO: US perps are live
items.idea: CFTC Chair Michael Selig approved Backpack for both a Designated Contract Market and a Derivatives Clearing Organization, allowing 24/7 leveraged crypto perps for Americans on one global order book with fiat and crypto collateral and cross-margin. tZERO got exchange approval a week earlier. This month the CFTC also cleared single-stock perps (Nov 3) and told exchanges they generally can't geoblock by state (Nov 5). All of it via staff action, with one sitting commissioner.
items.angle: Onshore perps erode offshore venues' US flow and pressure Hyperliquid's 'we're infrastructure' stance. BP token +20% shows the market pricing licensing as a moat.
items.tweetA: Single-stock perps on Nov 3. No state geoblocks on Nov 5. Onchain perps exchange and clearinghouse on Nov 16. The CFTC rebuilt US derivatives in two weeks with one commissioner and no legislation.
items.tweetB: Backpack's US president is a former CFTC commissioner. The first onchain perps license went to the venue whose leadership knows the agency. Regulatory capture is now a crypto competitive advantage.

items.title: Who's next: Hyperliquid says it's 'infrastructure', Lighter runs Robinhood's perps
items.idea: Jeff Yan argues Hyperliquid is infrastructure, and that regulators should oversee the HIP-3 deployers on top (ICE invested in Trade.xyz, Kraken's parent reportedly in talks). Backpack's direct registration weakens that argument. Lighter has run Robinhood Wallet's perps since July with a 50/50 revenue split and is seen as a likely next licensee. Hyperliquid led protocol revenue Monday at $2.61M.
items.angle: Two US routes are competing: register (Backpack) or partner (HIP-3, Lighter-Robinhood). Whoever wins defines how onchain derivatives reach US retail.
items.tweetA: Hyperliquid makes about $2.6M a day and says it isn't an exchange. Backpack just proved a crypto-native exchange can register. 'We're just infrastructure' gets harder to argue every week. $HYPE
items.tweetB: Lighter runs Robinhood's perps and had a $10M+ drain on Monday. It's the leading candidate for the next CFTC license. The timing of that post-mortem matters.

items.title: Warsh: Fed staff modeling three AI scenarios, including an investment bust
items.idea: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said staff are modeling three AI scenarios: a productivity boom shared with workers, a boom where automation outpaces hiring and unemployment rises, and an investment bust where returns disappoint and equity valuations fall. Trump also said he'd 'not mind' Jensen Huang returning; Nvidia's board says it isn't considering it.
items.angle: The Fed formally modeling an AI investment bust is new. It gives cover for a dovish pivot if the AI unwind spills into credit, even while the market prices hikes.
items.tweetA: The Fed chair now has an official 'AI investment bust' scenario. The central bank is modeling the downside the equity market spent two years ignoring.
items.tweetB: Three Warsh scenarios: shared boom, jobless boom, bust. Only one is good for workers, and only one is good for equities. They aren't the same one.

items.title: Situational Awareness 13F: $20.2B to $1.58B (-92%)
items.idea: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness reported its 13F portfolio fell 92% to $1.58B in Q3 from $20.2B, reflecting a forced unwind of public positions in July after steep losses on concentrated AI bets.
items.angle: The highest-conviction AI thesis fund was forced out in July, months before the November selloff. Forced sellers lead; retail (record QQQ inflow) follows.
items.tweetA: The fund named after the AI-is-coming essay went from $20B to $1.6B in a quarter. It was forced out in July. The AI selloff everyone noticed in November started in a 13F nobody read.
items.tweetB: Concentrated conviction plus leverage is the same failure mode in every cycle. Only the theme changes. Situational Awareness is the Archegos of the AI trade, without the bank losses (so far).

items.title: Strategy buys 485 BTC above spot, spends ~6x more buying back STRC preferred
items.idea: Strategy bought 485 BTC for about $33.4M at about $68,900 each, lifting holdings to 850,849 BTC, while repurchasing about $206-228M of STRC preferred. BTC is at $64.9k. BTC ETFs broke a 7-day outflow streak with +$8M; ETH ETFs -$8M. BitMine added 7,653 ETH to 6.08M (4.97% of supply), with Tom Lee blaming ETH's slide on Asian margin selling tied to Nvidia and cash-raising for Anthropic's IPO.
items.angle: Strategy spending 6x more defending its preferred stack than buying BTC is a capital-structure tell. The flywheel has shifted from accumulation to liability management.
items.tweetA: Strategy spent $33M on bitcoin and about $206M buying back its own preferred. When the bitcoin treasury company spends 6x more on its capital structure than on bitcoin, the flywheel has changed direction. $MSTR
items.tweetB: Tom Lee says ETH is falling because people are raising cash for the Anthropic IPO. If one AI IPO can move ETH 18% in two weeks, crypto is now a funding source for AI, not a hedge against it.

items.title: DTCC + Barclays: tokenization's real prize is idle collateral
items.idea: DTCC's Val Wooton and Barclays' Scott Lucas say tokenization's near-term prize is idle collateral. Firms over-fund and over-collateralize every day because assets get stuck when markets close, and 24/7 movement could save 'millions, if not billions'. Separately, Jupiter will allow borrowing against tokenized Bullish shares with onchain liquidations.
items.angle: Collateral mobility is the plumbing use case that can actually scale. It connects to Howell's collateral multiplier: faster collateral velocity is a liquidity source.
items.tweetA: The killer app for tokenization isn't retail stock trading. It's collateral that doesn't sit idle every weekend. DTCC says that's worth billions. That's Howell's collateral multiplier, delivered by blockchain.
items.tweetB: Every Friday at 5pm, trillions in collateral freeze until Monday, so firms over-post to cover the gap. 24/7 settlement releases that buffer. It's quiet QE through plumbing.

items.title: Zelle moves $1.25M of ZelleUSD between banks on Solana, amounts encrypted
items.idea: At Breakpoint, Zelle moved $1.25M of Anchorage-issued ZelleUSD between two banks on Solana, with the amount encrypted but the transfer verifiable. Solana dropped the 'mainnet beta' label for 'Solana 1.0' after Alpenglow (Oct 21) and Firedancer. The Solana Foundation also took a majority stake in CoinGecko.
items.angle: Bank-grade confidential transfers remove a key institutional blocker for public chains. Buying CoinGecko is a distribution play: owning the price page retail checks first.
items.tweetA: Zelle, the US bank network, moved a stablecoin between two banks on Solana with the amount hidden. Confidential payments on a public chain were the institutional blocker. One just went away. $SOL
items.tweetB: The Solana Foundation bought majority control of CoinGecko. Owning the price page millions check every day is a bigger moat than owning the fastest chain.

items.title: Ex-Robinhood engineer front-ran 11 listings on Hyperliquid perps for $125k
items.idea: Former Robinhood engineer Huaisong Xiang pleaded guilty to wire fraud for buying Hyperliquid perps ahead of at least 11 Robinhood Crypto listing announcements in 2025-2026, making $125,523, or about $11k per listing.
items.angle: Onchain perps are transparent enough to get insiders caught. The audit trail of 'unregulated' DEXs is now an enforcement tool.
items.tweetA: $11k per insider trade, 11 times, on a public blockchain. He got caught because the ledger is permanent. Onchain perps may be the worst venue in the world for insider trading.
items.tweetB: Prosecutors are now using Hyperliquid's public order flow as evidence. The 'offshore, unregulated' venue produced a cleaner audit trail than most TradFi brokers.

items.title: Optimizely hijacked: 188 scripts on 178 sites (Ledger, BBC, Zoom, HSBC), $7k stolen
items.idea: Attackers exploited website testing platform Optimizely to inject malicious code into 188 scripts across 178 organizations, including Ledger, the BBC, Zoom, HSBC, CNN and Salesforce. The drainer wallets collected only about $7,150.
items.angle: Third-party script supply chain risk is systemic. The low haul is luck, not security. It's a cyber-vendor talking point for $NET and $CRWD-type client-side protection.
items.tweetA: One A/B testing vendor gave attackers code execution on HSBC, Zoom, Salesforce and Ledger at the same time. They stole $7k. Next time the payload won't be a crypto drainer.
items.tweetB: 178 companies trusted a marketing script with full page access. The real attack surface of a bank's website is whatever growth-team tool was added last quarter.

items.title: Lighter drain: a trader's homemade signer reused nonces and leaked the key
items.idea: Lighter froze withdrawals after a wallet pulled $10.39M USDC (0xTria estimates about $15.5M across two market-maker accounts). Lighter blames one trader's custom signing software, which skipped official SDKs and reused nonces, letting the attacker derive the key from public signatures and route funds via a public pool. About $5M was returned. Lighter now requires wallet signatures for pool deposits and stopped exposing API-key signatures.
items.angle: The bug is in a client, not the protocol, but the exchange design (public signatures, pool transfers) made it exploitable. It's a due-diligence point as Lighter courts a CFTC license.
items.tweetA: Lighter lost $10M+ because a market maker wrote its own signer and reused a nonce, the same mistake that broke the PS3's ECDSA in 2010. Crypto keeps relearning 15-year-old cryptography. $LIT
items.tweetB: The exchange says the hack wasn't its fault. It also changed two of its own design choices afterwards. Both can be true, and the CFTC will be reading the post-mortem either way.

items.title: Trezor's second shipping-partner breach: 27k home addresses, 'someone shows up at the door'
items.idea: Trezor shipping partner Skladon was breached on Nov 7, exposing about 27,000 orders (Aug 9-Nov 7): names, phones, emails, addresses and what each customer bought. It's the second fulfilment breach since August (after ShipMonk). Scam calls have started, and Trezor's CCO warned 'in the worst case, someone shows up at the door'. Trezor cut data retention to 45 days and launched nickname-only pickup in 18 EU countries.
items.angle: Physical 'wrench attack' risk for self-custodians is now a supply chain problem. That's a structural argument for institutional custody and multisig with geographic distribution.
items.tweetA: A list of 27,000 home addresses of people who just bought a crypto hardware wallet has leaked. This is a physical security problem, not a cyber one.
items.tweetB: Self-custody's weakest link isn't the seed phrase. It's the logistics company that knows which house the wallet was shipped to. Two breaches in three months.

items.title: SCOTUS kills Custodia's Fed master-account case after six years
items.idea: The Supreme Court declined to hear Custodia Bank's challenge to the Fed's master-account denial, leaving the 10th Circuit ruling that the Kansas City Fed had discretion as final. Custodia first applied in October 2020. Judge Tymkovich's dissent had warned that 'without a master account, a bank cannot operate'. Kraken Financial got a limited-purpose account this year.
items.angle: Direct Fed access stays discretionary, which keeps crypto banks dependent on sponsor banks. Kraken's limited-purpose path becomes the template.
items.tweetA: Six years, three courts, no master account. The Fed decides who gets to be a bank, and courts won't second-guess it. Crypto's route into the payment system goes through Kraken's narrow door.
items.tweetB: Stablecoins got a law. Crypto banks didn't get a Fed account. The US is fine with dollar tokens but not with crypto firms holding reserves at the Fed directly.

items.title: MEV brothers acquitted: exploiting code isn't wire fraud without a misrepresentation
items.idea: Judge Jessica Clarke acquitted the Peraire-Bueno brothers on remaining charges over the $25M 2023 Ethereum MEV exploit, ruling prosecutors never identified a material misrepresentation, which wire fraud requires. Their first trial ended in a mistrial.
items.angle: It narrows the DOJ's 'code is fraud' theory. That's precedent for MEV and smart-contract exploit cases (Mango-style). Builders and searchers get more legal room.
items.tweetA: $25M taken from MEV bots, and no fraud, because nobody was lied to. The court just said exploiting a protocol's rules isn't the same as deceiving a person. That's a big line for DeFi.
items.tweetB: If gaming code isn't wire fraud, the only protection DeFi has is better code. That raises the value of audits and formal verification, and lowers the value of 'we'll call the FBI'.

items.title: Schiff + 8 senators vs CFTC's order banning prediction-market state geoblocks
items.idea: Sen. Adam Schiff and eight Democratic senators asked the CFTC to scrap its Nov 5 order telling prediction markets to drop state geoblocks within 30 days, arguing it conflicts with active court orders. They want a reply from Selig by Nov 23.
items.angle: Federal preemption of state gambling law is the core fight for $HOOD, Kalshi and Polymarket's US growth. The Nov 23 date and early-December deadline are near-term catalysts.
items.tweetA: The CFTC told prediction markets to stop blocking states. Nine senators say that conflicts with court orders. That's federal preemption vs state gambling law, and the reply is due Nov 23. $HOOD
items.tweetB: One CFTC commissioner is preempting 50 state gaming regulators by staff order. Whatever happens, it ends up in front of a judge.

items.title: Safe multisig loses $6.4M through permissions its owners set
items.idea: A Safe multisig lost $6.4M after a likely compromised key sent a transaction its owners' custom Zodiac Roles Modifier permissions allowed. Safe and Zodiac both say their code had no flaw.
items.angle: Same pattern as Lighter: secure core, insecure configuration. Treasury ops risk is now about permissions design, not smart contracts.
items.tweetA: Two crypto losses this week, $10M and $6.4M, and in both the protocol code was fine. The money left through settings someone configured. The attack surface is ops, not code.
items.tweetB: Multisig only works if every role is set up correctly. One permissive module turned a 'secure' treasury into a single-key wallet.

items.title: Vitalik backs leanPCS: quantum-safe Ethereum signatures as one aggregate proof per block
items.idea: Vitalik Buterin backed a leanPCS design for EIP-8288, which would fold quantum-safe signatures into one aggregate proof per block instead of posting them all onchain. He says it can ship sooner because it only requires choosing a mathematical field.
items.angle: Post-quantum migration is an underpriced chain risk. A credible faster path is a relative positive for ETH versus chains without a roadmap (BTC's PQ debate is slower).
items.tweetA: Post-quantum signatures are huge, so Ethereum's plan is not to post them: aggregate a whole block's worth into one proof. Ethereum is starting its quantum migration before Bitcoin.
items.tweetB: Every chain will need quantum-safe signatures. The question is who pays the blockspace. Vitalik's answer is to compress it with proofs. The ZK roadmap just became the security roadmap.

items.title: Germany: customs can seize assets over €100k of unclear origin without suspicion
items.idea: The Bundestag passed a bill letting customs secure assets of unclear origin over €100,000, crypto included, without any criminal suspicion. The federal bar association BRAK warned that missing proof of origin, for example on inherited wealth, could be treated as evidence of illegality.
items.angle: This reverses the burden of proof for wealth in Europe's largest economy. It's a capital-flight and self-custody demand signal, and a test case for EU AML expansion.
items.tweetA: Germany now lets customs freeze €100k+ if you can't prove where it came from. No suspicion needed. Inherited a Bitcoin wallet from your father? Hope you kept the receipts.
items.tweetB: The burden of proof on wealth just flipped in Europe's biggest economy. Every time a state does this, demand for assets it can't easily see goes up.

items.title: DBS + JPM Kinexys 24/7 tokenized USD deposits US-Singapore; MAS + Bundesbank wCBDC FX test
items.idea: DBS and JPMorgan's Kinexys linked their blockchain deposit networks for 24/7 instant cross-border tokenized USD transfers between the US and Singapore. Ant International is the first client, using it for real-time treasury. Separately, MAS and the Bundesbank tested EUR/SGD settlement with wholesale CBDCs (Project Simbolon), using ZK proofs so neither ledger links directly.
items.angle: Bank tokenized deposits, not stablecoins, are winning corporate treasury. The Ant International client is notable given US-China friction.
items.tweetA: JPMorgan and DBS just made dollar deposits move 24/7 between New York and Singapore. The first client is Ant, a Chinese fintech. Tokenized dollars are reaching Chinese balance sheets through banks.
items.tweetB: Two central banks settled FX with ZK proofs so neither had to trust the other's ledger. That's the architecture for de-dollarized settlement, and it's being built by the Bundesbank, not the BRICS.

items.title: Toss to give ~30M Koreans a non-custodial ETH/USDT/USDC wallet
items.idea: Toss is preparing a non-custodial wallet for its roughly 30 million South Korean users, launching on Ethereum with ETH, USDT and USDC, with fee-free sends to phone contacts.
items.angle: 30M is close to 60% of South Korea's 51.7M population. It's a distribution shock for USD stablecoins in a market where KRW stablecoins are being debated.
items.tweetA: Toss has about 30M users, nearly 60% of South Korea. It's about to put USDT and USDC wallets on all of them. Korea's won-stablecoin debate may be settled by dollar distribution first.
items.tweetB: Upbit's revenue fell 61% the same week Korea's top fintech app launched self-custody. Retail crypto in Korea may be moving from exchanges to wallets.

items.title: Upbit operator Dunamu: Q3 revenue -61%, swings to loss
items.idea: Dunamu posted a Q3 net loss of 18.6B won (about $14M) as revenue fell 61% y/y to 151.7B won, against 239B won of profit a year ago.
items.angle: Korean retail volume is a leading indicator for alt liquidity. A 61% revenue drop says the 'kimchi bid' is gone.
items.tweetA: Upbit revenue down 61% y/y and a loss. Korean retail was the marginal alt buyer in every cycle. They've left the room.
items.tweetB: Dunamu earned 239B won a year ago and lost 18.6B won this quarter. Exchange revenue is the purest read on retail crypto appetite, and it's in recession.

items.title: Treasury-company marks: Evernorth XRP -60% vs cost; Cypherpunk's ZEC mining pays
items.idea: Ripple-backed Evernorth wrote its 346M XRP down to $341.9M, about 60% below its $846.6M cost (roughly $0.99 vs $2.45 per coin). Winklevoss-backed Cypherpunk swung to $2.6M operating income on $9.9M of Zcash mining revenue and bought 3,776 ZEC at $920 after the quarter (quarter-end price $1,415). Strive bought 251 BTC at about $69,853, to 43,404 BTC.
items.angle: The digital-asset-treasury model breaks when underlying assets drop 60%. The few with operating cash flow (mining) are the ones still standing.
items.tweetA: Evernorth paid $2.45 per XRP and marks it at $0.99. A listed treasury company down 60% on its only asset in its first quarter. The DAT trade is turning into the SPAC trade. $XRP
items.tweetB: Cypherpunk is the rare crypto treasury company with operating income, because it mines ZEC instead of only holding it. Owning the means of production still beats owning the coin.

items.title: Boris Johnson backs tokenization, eight months after calling Bitcoin a Ponzi
items.idea: At Solana Breakpoint, Boris Johnson backed asset tokenization and London's push to lead on blockchain, eight months after calling bitcoin a Ponzi scheme in the Daily Mail. He stayed wary of speculation and questioned how theft victims recover funds.
items.angle: The UK political class is pivoting to 'blockchain not bitcoin' on tokenization. That's a policy tailwind for UK market-infrastructure players.
items.tweetA: From 'bitcoin is a Ponzi' to keynoting a Solana conference in eight months. Politicians follow the speaking fees, and tokenization is where the fees are.
items.tweetB: The London pitch is now 'tokenization yes, speculation no'. That's how a financial centre adopts the plumbing while disowning the casino.
